explicit_propositions.text: The Fairhaven Project was a joint conflict resolution initiative between the Northeast Maritime Institute and the U.S. State Department.
The project aimed to foster mutual understanding and reduce conflict through shared living experiences.
The project brought together Israeli and Palestinian high school students.
Participants lived aboard the sailing vessel Fritha for three weeks.
The Fairhaven Project lasted approximately five to six years.
Living together required participants to co-cook, clean, and learn to sail the vessel.
The speaker experienced anxiety about living alongside Israelis due to lack of prior direct contact.
The speaker grew up in a leftist household that valued peace and coexistence.
Both Israeli and Palestinian students likely held media-influenced perceptions of the other side.
After the Fairhaven Program, the speaker’s father sponsored their education in economics and natural building.

assumptions.text: True conflict resolution requires intimate, prolonged interpersonal interaction beyond abstract dialogue.
Shared physical labor fosters empathy and reduces dehumanization of perceived enemies.
Peacebuilding at the grassroots level can be more transformative than top-down diplomatic efforts.
Personal relationships formed during cross-cultural programs can lead to lasting professional and civic impacts.
Structural inequality persists despite formal equality, requiring targeted intervention to achieve equity.
Capacity-building in marginalized communities is more sustainable than external aid delivery.
Local ownership of solutions increases effectiveness and longevity of development initiatives.
Systemic oppression thrives when narratives of victimhood are dismissed or delegitimized.
Democratic institutions require genuine engagement with dissenting voices to remain legitimate.
Technological innovation in global health must prioritize simplicity, maintainability, and context-specific adaptation.
